meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: That's right.
You said it right.

examples.text: Это правильно. Я приглашаю вас в общественный совет.
examples.trans: That's right. I'm inviting you onto the public council.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нять'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to understand', paired with 'понимать'.

examples.trans: I didn't understand.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?
I understand you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мочь'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to be able, to manage', paired with 'мочь'.

examples.trans: We came as soon as we could.
Will you be able to come tomorrow morning?

examples.text: Я думаю, что у меня есть мужчина. Он сможет меня защитить.
examples.trans: I think that I have a man. He will be able to protect me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to come', paired with 'прийти'.

examples.trans: Come tomorrow.
He comes every day.
If you change your mind, come back. The job is waiting.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'all right, OK', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go.
OK, I'm coming.
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'let's go'.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?
Not allowed? All right, I'll go and do my homework.
All right, let's go to our room.

набрать.gloss: to gather, rack up (views/points); to dial

meanings.en: to gather, rack up (views/points); to dial
meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'брать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to gather, rack up (views/points); to dial', paired with 'набирать'.

examples.text: Ролик уже набрал четыре миллиона просмотров!
examples.trans: The clip has already got four million views!
I'll dial your number.

examples.text: Мы наберём много лайков в интернете.
examples.trans: We will gather many likes on the internet.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common masculine noun meaning 'fridge' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The milk is in the fridge.
Whose fridge is this?

examples.text: Курица? Нет. А чей это холодильник?
examples.trans: Chicken? No. And whose fridge is this?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

examples.text: А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: International compound from Greek 'tele' (far) + 'phone' (voice, sound).

examples.trans: Give me the phone.
Where's my phone?

examples.text: Мне нужно позвонить губернатору. Дай телефон.
examples.trans: I need to call the governor. Give me a phone.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'терять'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to lose', paired with 'терять'.

examples.trans: I've lost my key.
Have you lost all fear?

examples.text: Что смотрите, бандерлоги? Вы совсем страх потеряли?
examples.trans: What are you staring at, you monkeys? Have you lost all fear?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: What are you doing?
I'm making dinner.
Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'juice' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Orange juice.
I will drink a little good juice.
Make me some fresh orange juice.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'верное').

examples.trans: Well, probably somewhere in the archive.
He has probably already come home.

examples.text: Наверное, что-то серьёзное у вас. Девочка уже две недели лежит в областной клинике!
examples.trans: It must be something serious for you. The girl has been lying in the regional clinic for two weeks already!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.
Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

придумать.gloss: to think up, to come up with

meanings.en: to think up, to come up with
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'думать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to think up, to come up with', paired with 'придумывать'.

examples.trans: You came up with this yourself!
I'll think up a plan.

examples.text: Как нет? Ты же сам это всё придумал!
examples.trans: What do you mean, no time? You came up with all this yourself!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Of course I'll help.
Yes, of course.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лово'). Common neuter noun meaning 'word' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: But you gave your word!
He keeps his word.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

следить.gloss: to watch, to follow; to keep an eye on

meanings.en: to watch, to follow; to keep an eye on
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ледить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to watch, to follow; to keep an eye on', paired with 'проследить'.

examples.trans: Are you watching us?
Keep an eye on the child.
What, are you watching us?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'sheep' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: A white sheep is grazing in the field.
You are a foolish sheep yourself, got it?

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'ткнуться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to shut up'.

related.gloss: not to to shut up (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: Shut up and keep working.

examples.text: Заткнись, Вика, я никогда не делаю ошибок!
examples.trans: Shut up, Vika, I never make mistakes!

examples.text: Заткнись, рыжая, не мешай мне спокойно работать!
examples.trans: Shut up, redhead, do not disturb me working peacefully!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'dwarf, gnome' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Who's a dwarf? I'm a dwarf?
Seven dwarfs lived in the fairy tale.
Listen here, you dwarf! Go away from here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'already', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.
Dad is already home.
I'm already home.

обниматься.gloss: to hug each other, to embrace

meanings.en: to hug each other, to embrace
meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ниматься'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hug each other, to embrace', paired with 'обняться'.

examples.trans: Why are you two hugging?

examples.text: Что вы обнимаетесь? Вы с ума сошли!
examples.trans: Why are you two hugging? Have you lost your minds!

examples.text: Да, под такую музыку обниматься немного неловко.
examples.trans: Yes, it is a bit awkward hugging to such music.
